tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

102	gh api -X PUT repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async -f merge_method=squash \
103	  -f commit_title="<subject> (#<n>)" -f commit_message="<the What, as prose>" -f sha=<head sha>
104	gh api repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async/<uuid>      # poll until "merged"
105	```

Your local copy of that branch is now behind a rewritten remote — check the trees are identical (`git diff --quiet origin/<b> <b>`) and `git reset --hard origin/<b>`. Then wait for checks and merge.
110	2. **A child carrying merge commits is not restacked.** Two cases:
111	   - *It is a strict superset of `main`* (it merged its parents in as they were first written). Prove it — the merged pull requests' original tips are ancestors, and `git diff --stat origin/main HEAD` lists only this pull request's files. A plain `git merge origin/main` will conflict on every file both sides touched (add/add against the squashed copies), so record the merge with `git merge -s ours origin/main`, confirm the tree did not change, push, `gh pr edit <n> --base main`.
112	   - *It is not a superset* (main moved for other reasons). `git rebase --onto origin/main <old-parent-tip> <branch>`, confirm `git diff --stat <reviewed-tip> HEAD -- <your dirs>` is empty, `git push --force-with-lease`, `gh pr edit <n> --base main`.
113	3. **Run a join check before merging the second of two parallel stacks**: both test suites and the end-to-end test on the rebased top branch. In stack 03 it caught an end-to-end assertion that typed in a fixture number the other stack had changed.
114	4. **After changing a pull request's base by hand, GitHub can keep a stale `CONFLICTING` and schedule no checks at all** (stack 04, #39): confirm `gh pr view <n> --json mergeable` is `MERGEABLE` and that `gh pr checks <n>` lists jobs BEFORE waiting on them; if not, `gh pr close <n> && gh pr reopen <n>` makes it recompute and run CI. GitHub also did not restack a child whose branch had been force-pushed — use the `rebase --onto` route above and prove the tree is identical to the reviewed tip.
115	5. Afterwards: delete branches locally and with `gh api -X DELETE repos/kgang/katalyst/git/refs/heads/<branch>`, `git worktree remove` each worktree, `git fetch --prune`. Leave the `entire/*` branches alone — they are the checkpoint tool's.
116	
117	---
118	
119	## 6. Your environment (checked 2026-09-17)
120	
121	| Tool | Version here | Note |
122	|------|--------------|------|
123	| `gh` | 2.101.0, signed in as `kgang` | Repo `kgang/katalyst`, private |
124	| `uv` | 0.12.15 | |
125	| Python | 3.12.4 | |
126	| Node | 23.3.0 locally | Docker and CI pin **24**. Use `npm ci`, not `npm install`, in a fresh worktree |
127	| Docker | 27.5.1 | |
128	| Playwright | `@playwright/test` in `frontend/` | `npx playwright install chromium` once; `npx playwright test` starts both halves itself |
129	
130	**`.env` in the main checkout is Kent's.** It is git-ignored and holds his real keys. **Never copy it into a worktree, never read it into a brief, never commit it.** `.env.example` is the one agents use.
131	
132	**Hooks:** `.claude/settings.json` runs the `entire` checkpoint tool on session events; its output on `git push` is normal. The git hooks directory has a `commit-msg` hook but **no `pre-commit` hook wired**, so the linters do not run on commit — run `uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check .` and `npm run lint` yourself before committing.
133	
134	**Model API key: stack 04b needs one to record cassettes and demos — and Kent must name a spending ceiling first.** Before writing *any* code that calls Claude, load the `claude-api` skill; decision record 0006 holds the verified specifics, and memory is unreliable. Continuous integration never gets a key.
135	
136	**Running the app to look at it:** backend `cd backend && env -u ANTHROPIC_API_KEY -u FRED_API_KEY uv run uvicorn katalyst.api.main:app --port 80NN`; frontend `KATALYST_API_URL=http://localhost:80NN npm run dev -- --port 51NN --strictPort`. Give each agent its own pair of ports. For screenshots, a throwaway Playwright script **outside the repo** (the session scratchpad) at 1600 × 1000.
137	
138	---
139	
140	## 7. The worktree pattern
141	
142	Every sub-agent gets its own checkout of its own branch under **`../katalyst-wt/<branch-slug>/`**. The main checkout stays on `main` and is never used by a sub-agent.
143	
144	- **One agent per worktree**, except chapter writers, who may share one **only** when their files are disjoint and **none of them runs a git command** — the coordinator commits for them.
145	- **Disjoint owned files**, listed in the brief. "Touch nothing outside it. If something outside it must change, write why in your report."
146	- **Agents never push, never open a pull request, never touch `main`.** The coordinator reviews, then pushes and opens the pull request.
147	- A resumed agent (send it a message) keeps its context — use that for fix rounds and for sweeps of files it wrote. You can point a resumed agent at a *different* worktree when the fix has to land on another branch.
148	- Remove worktrees after the merge.
149	
150	---
151	
152	## 8. Lessons — read these twice
153	
154	1. **After any interruption, check reality before acting.** `git log --oneline -5`, `git status`, `git worktree list`, `gh pr list`, and `STATUS.md`. Do not trust your memory of the repo; trust the repo.
155	2. **Append to `STATUS.md` before you stop**, and whenever the set of open pull requests or running agents changes. Record Kent's instructions there in his own words.
156	3. **Brief sub-agents fully, and point at the one copy.** They know only what you tell them. Give the plan and the decisions note by **absolute path in the main checkout** (readable from any worktree) rather than pasting tables — no transcription drift. Paste only what must be word for word on screen.
157	4. **Keep cross-references consistent.** After any rename or any changed number, search the whole repo. A fixture change in stack 03 made numbers stale in eight chapters, the PRD, a decision record and an end-to-end test.
158	5. **Whoever changes a fixture or an engine rule lists which chapter numbers went stale, and the sweep travels in the same pull request.** Resume the chapter's own writer for the sweep.
159	6. **Verify every sub-agent's claim yourself.** Run the tests and lints, read the diff against the owned-files list, hand-check arithmetic on a tiny map of your own, **launch the app and look**. A report is a hypothesis. In stack 03 this caught: a lint failure an agent reported as green, a plate overlap on a map the agent had not probed, and a fixed-height tile full of dead space.
160	7. **Write the shapes sheet before parallel writers start** — and for parallel stacks, the event or type vocabulary they share.
161	8. **Put a read-only reviewer over parallel writers, every time.** It found about ten blocking cross-chapter disagreements per stack — two names for one type, the same test named two ways, "six options" over a list of five, a block of invented numbers. Have it **re-do every worked number by hand from the fixture**.
162	9. **Two honest principles settle most small questions**: one rule over two (find the rule the code already obeys and name it once); and a code, a word or a number must mean what it says (that is why there is `edit_not_applicable`, why `killed` means only forced false, why the chip says "stated range · not computed").
163	10. **Never put a typed-in number where a computed one belongs — including in tests.** Assert directions, orderings and states; or compare a value with itself across a change.
164	11. **Property tests must build their inputs.** One that `assume()`s most inputs away fails Hypothesis's health check in CI on a bad seed while passing locally. CI is about 2.5× slower than this machine.
165	12. **The first pull request of a stack is small enough to write yourself**: commit chapter *stubs* (headings only) so code agents can branch off the spec branch at once.
166	13. **Opus agents can hit a session limit** ("resets 7am America/New_York"). If one dies, check disk state before reviving it by message.
167	15. **A client library accepting a shape proves nothing about the service.** In stack 04 the SDK built a schema from a union of three shapes without complaint and the service refused it on the first live call (`For 'anyOf', '$defs' is not supported`). Only a live call settles a vendor question — make the first one early, make it small, and do not close a chapter's open question on the library's say-so.
168	16. **Test a program as a program, and make a paid run impossible to lose.** Twice in stack 04 a run that cost money kept nothing: once because the recorder threw the receipt away with a file it would not write, once because the module's `__main__` guard sat above a function it called — invisible to every test (tests import, so everything is defined first) and to ruff and mypy. Run each `python -m` entry point in a subprocess test through its whole path; keep anything paid for incrementally, so a crash still leaves a file.
169	17. **A rare test failure is a bug until the evidence says otherwise.** Four times in stack 04 an agent's first instinct was "flaky — clear the example database": the keyboard left behind on a rebuilt tile; two keys in one frame; a locality leak through the day grid (a claim in a separate piece of the map moved by `.096`); a second through one global survival mask (`.083`). Every one was a real defect a user could hit. Find the falsifying input, rebuild it by hand, and decide with evidence whether the test or the product is wrong. And pytest TRUNCATES a repr — `Belief(p=1.85...` is `1.85e-05`, not a likelihood above 1.
170	18. **Several worktrees on one machine share one set of end-to-end ports.** Until stack 04 fixed it, `frontend/playwright.config.ts` used fixed ports and reused any server already up, so one agent's `npx playwright test` silently tested another branch's app — and "verified" numbers were wrong in both directions. Give every agent, and yourself, explicit ports (`KATALYST_E2E_BACKEND_PORT`, `KATALYST_E2E_FRONTEND_PORT`), never reuse a server, and never edit a source file under a running dev server (a hot reload blanks the page mid-test and looks like your change broke everything).
171	19. **One queue for heavy work, enforced by a script, not by asking.** Stack 04's first session ran three or four suites and 40× repeat bars at once; the load sat at 20–23 and the load itself caused failures that were then chased. `plans/scripts/heavy.sh` is a lock directory holding its owner's process id: whoever asks waits their turn. Agents run single test files, linters and type checks directly; a whole suite through the queue; playwright, repeat bars and anything paid are the coordinator's alone. Two 600-run bars and four agents' suites went through it on 2026-09-21 without one spurious failure.
172	20. **100% coverage and 259 green tests proved nothing about whether the arithmetic was right.** Three defects sat on the demo map — an observation that never reached a cause, endings deaf to half their causes, a supposition voided by a claim nobody believed — because no test compared the engine with an answer worked out independently, under an edit. Every engine needs an oracle that is *forbidden the engine's internals*, the way the locality oracle may not call `affected_set`. And check what an oracle can see: one that shares the core's tables proves the summing and is blind to a wrong table.
173	21. **Attack a plan before its owner sees it, and re-check a review before acting on it.** The two midpoint reviews read a `main` ten pull requests old: of one audit's blockers, six were already fixed, and one review's central claim about generation (the map is a tree) was false by measurement. Then the coordinator's own synthesis said "solved exactly" where an adversarial pass measured .12 of error, offered Kent a choice that was not optional, and under-counted the work by about 1.6×. One read-only red-team agent, told to break it, cost twenty minutes. A design that rests on a prototype opens with a spike and a kill criterion. And keep the evidence: an analyst's scripts go in `plans/analysis/scripts/`, not a temp directory.
174	22. **A green bar here is not a green bar there — and more runs of the same bar is not the answer.** On 2026-09-21 a replay test passed 20 cold runs of 20 on this machine and failed the build's FIRST run: the layout is worked out on its own thread, the build machine's thread was slower, and a claim took a rectangle's place at the origin. Throttling the processor did not reproduce it (that slows the page, not the layout thread); starting the layout thread 900 ms late did, at once. The same day a generated numbers file matched byte for byte across macOS/Arm and Linux/x86-64 — and its own margin test still went red on Linux, because with 280 numbers some value sits on a rounding boundary on some machine at ANY digit count. **Rules:** a test that reads a MOMENT (what stood when X arrived) gets a no-browser twin that injects the bad timing on purpose; a check that compares NUMBERS uses a stated tolerance, never text; and the amount of browser testing follows the three tiers in `PLAN.md`'s working rules — one cold run and the build by default, a repeat bar only for a rare failure that has actually been seen. The "20 cold runs" bar was never a recorded standard; it cost about fifty-two minutes that day (twice in full, a third time to five runs of twenty) and caught nothing one run plus the build would not have.
175	23. **The whole suite, through the queue, before EVERY push; and never edit a worktree while a bar is running in it.** Both broken once on 2026-09-21: a push after two test files let three stale health tests reach the build (#41's first run); an edit under a running bar hot-reloaded a fix into its dev server and voided three runs. Check `plans/.heavy.log` for an open START before touching a worktree.
176	24. **A defect an agent "fixed" without a browser is a hypothesis — revert the fix and watch the test go red before believing either.** Stack 04's polish branch boasted that its new layout check *"found its first defect before it was ever run"*: three fields overflowing the panel. With both "fixes" reverted the fields still sat inside it — `width: 100%` had always been there — and the check written to catch the overflow could not have seen one (the panel scrolls sideways, so scrolling a field into view made it measure as inside). Four deliberate breakages through the queue settled both in ten minutes.
177	25. **Anything paid is kept OUTSIDE the worktree that ran it.** `KATALYST_RUNS=/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/backend/.runs`. The raw run behind the committed Hormuz recording died with a removed worktree, and `docs/measurements.md` has to say so. And a program that writes its kept run only when a case ENDS loses it to a hard kill.
178	26. **Before writing "X says why", open X.** In one evening the coordinator wrote that a scorecard row named its effort (it did not — only the kept run did) and glossed a stop reason from its name (`width_cap` is not "the map reached its widest"). Both were caught only by looking. A sentence about what a file holds is a claim like any other.
179	27. **The suite had never met a live run, a keyed first screen, or a generated map — and Kent met all three in his first five minutes.** Every browser test plays a recording at 0.4 s an event, with an empty key, over the one curated map where every number exists. So a dead `?` key, a minute of silence after pressing *Watch it build*, a recording unreachable with a key, and 36 empty cells of 54 on the tiles were all invisible to 1 000 green tests. **Walk the product the way its owner will — with the key in, on a map nobody curated — before calling a stack done.** And when analysts plan the fix, put what the owner literally asked for on the table at full strength beside their alternative: three of four had quietly argued him out of it, and an adversarial pass re-counted their ~12 sessions at ~25.
180	14. **Say what you merged and why before Kent has to ask**, and if you take a step earlier than he literally asked (stack 03a was merged while 03b's last pull request was still being built), tell him plainly and offer to hold.
181	
182	---
183	
184	## 9. The road from here
185	
186	| Stack | What it proves | Plan |
187	|-------|----------------|------|
188	| ~~01 skeleton~~ · ~~02 schema~~ | **Merged.** | history |
189	| ~~03a engine ∥ 03b canvas~~ | **Merged 2026-09-17.** Changing one step re-computes only what is downstream; the map is dense, readable and keyboard-driven | `stack-03a-engine.md`, `stack-03b-canvas.md` (history) |
190	| ~~04a join + growth ∥ 04b generation~~ | **Merged; closed 2026-09-21** (`history/stack-04-generation.md`). The canvas shows the engine's numbers; the model draws a real map for any hypothesis, streamed step by step; with no key the four examples replay | `stack-04-generation.md` |
191	| 05 thesis | The map compiles to a trade with a derived stop-loss and live market prices | `roadmap-03-to-06.md` |
192	| 06 probes | Extra modeling effort where the user points it (stretch) | `roadmap-03-to-06.md` |
193	| 07 presentable (proposed) | README walkthrough, a pastcast self-test, a last accessibility sweep | `roadmap-03-to-06.md` |
194	
195	**This table is history as of 2026-09-21. Start with `PLAN.md`** — stacks 05, 06 and 07 mean different things now, and several of their lines wait on Kent (`notes/2026-09-21-decisions-after-review.md`).

# HANDOFF — take over Katalyst and carry it to a working prototype

You are a fresh agent. You have no memory of how this project got here. This file gives you everything you need to continue. Read it fully, then read `STATUS.md` (newest entry on top), then **`PLAN.md`**.

> **2026-09-21, late — stack 04 is CLOSED and three lines of work run at once. Start from `RESUME-ux-round.md`.**
>
> **2026-09-21 — the road changed; this file's §2 and §9 describe the project before it did.** Two independent reviews were digested that day. They found three real defects in the engine's arithmetic on the demo map, and that the trade the brief ends in has no code. The road is now: finish stack 04 → **05 sound numbers, then settled shapes** → **06 the trade** → **07 a map you can argue with**. Read **`PLAN.md`** (what, in what order, the definition of done), **`design-after-midpoint-review.md`** (why), and **`notes/2026-09-21-decisions-after-review.md`** (Kent's decisions, R1 onward — binding; he answered every question the same day, and more have been added since). §4–§8 below — how Kent works, git, the environment, worktrees, the lessons — are unchanged and binding. Three working rules are new: **every whole suite, browser run and repeat bar goes through `plans/scripts/heavy.sh`, one at a time — it works across sessions**; **how much browser testing a change needs is decision record 0008's dated amendment (three tiers), not "20 cold runs"**; and **only Hormuz is recorded until the one shape freeze at the end of stack 05, when all four are recorded once (R9).**

---

## 1. The mission

Build **Katalyst**: a take-home prototype for Catalyst (catalyst.app), a seed-stage company that turns a trading idea stated in plain English into live execution.

**What the tool does, in one sentence:** you type an event you think will happen; Katalyst shows what it would cause, step by step, ending in trades — and lets you change any step to see how the trades change.

The brief is `ASSIGNMENT.md`. The owner is **Kent Gang**, a solo developer. He cares most about four things, in his words: well structured with Docker and tests; proper code design; rigorously documented decisions; and a beautiful, elegant, delightful interface.

**"Done" means:** a reviewer clones the repo, runs one command, and walks the full flow on all four example events from the brief — type a hypothesis, watch the cause-and-effect map draw itself, change a step, compare the two versions, and end on a thesis card with a derived stop-loss. Tests pass with no API key. Every number on screen can show why. Full checklist: `roadmap-03-to-06.md`, "Definition of done" (the boxes stack 03 ticked are ticked).

---

## 2. What is built, as of 2026-09-17 (end of stack 03)

Stacks 01 (skeleton), 02 (schema), **03a (engine) and 03b (canvas)** are merged to `main`. Every pull request up to #27 is squash-merged (a few numbers were never used), and `main` is green on five checks.

**The one sentence to hold on to:** *the engine computes everything and the canvas draws everything, and they have not met.* The canvas reads the stored example and shows every computed number as an absence with a reason ("no engine yet"). Joining them is the first code of stack 04.

**Documents.** `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md`; `ARCHITECTURE.md` (every section says *built* or *planned*); fourteen decision records in `docs/adr/`, **0001–0014, all accepted** — next is **0015**. The spec is a book: `spec/graph/` (4 chapters), `spec/multiverse/` (4: `interventions`, `branches-and-worlds`, `propagation`, `diff`), `spec/workbench/` (6: `color-motion-type`, `tiles-ports-wires`, `layout-and-zoom`, `keyboard-and-access`, `diff-view`, `inspector`, plus the landing page's **worked example cast** and **twelve-line visual review checklist**), and `spec/vocabulary.md` with its **Interface words** table and **Words for a number that is not there**. `spec/generation/` and `spec/thesis/` are landing pages only.

**The server** — `backend/src/katalyst/`:

- `domain/` — the pure core, twelve files, 100% covered, `mypy --strict` clean. Models (`belief`, `proposition`, `link`, `graph`, `intervention`, `branch`, `ids`), `validity.py` (`validate` returns every fault at once; **nineteen codes**: fourteen map faults, four refused edits, one refused comparison), **`patch.py`** (`Assignment`, `apply`, `flatten`, `affected_set`, `introduced_by`), **`propagation.py`** (`World`, `Retraction`, `SeriesState`, `propagate`, `versions_of` — two thousand versions of the map × eight worlds; a supposition is a hard fact until undermined; two seed streams derived per claim), **`diff.py`** (`diff`, `DeltaRow`, `sensitivity` — `shifted` read off the paired difference; rank = size of move × weakest arrow on the best-backed route).
- `engine/` — `ids.py` (the only place an identifier is made) and `worlds.py` (the only place that knows a store or a date). Nothing has ever called a model.
- `fixtures/hormuz.py` — the worked example, now **curated**: two inputs tuned and marked **Tuned**, and every `beliefs.model` equal to its `prior` ("nothing computed yet"). Branch `br_hormuz_then_strike`.
- `api/` — `GET /api/healthz`, `/readyz`, `/about`, `/fixtures`, `/fixtures/{id}`, and **`POST /api/worlds`, `/api/worlds/diff`, `/api/worlds/conditional`** (a refused branch is a 422 carrying every violation). Try: `curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/worlds -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"base_id":"hormuz","seed":20261001}'`.
- `grounding/` — an empty package (stack 05).

**The browser app** — `frontend/src/`: `api/schema.ts` (generated, never hand-edited) and `api/client.ts`; `world/` (the `WorldSource` seam, `FixtureWorldSource` live, **`ApiWorldSource` a stub waiting for stack 04**, hand-written `WorldView`, `branchReducer`); `graph/` (canvas, ELK layout on a background thread with pinning, `wires/` with routing and one-pass plate placement, `diff/` with the four structural states); `components/` (Tile, BeliefChip, OriginMark, Inspector, PathBar, DeltaRail, BranchPanel, Outline, CommandPalette, ShortcutsSheet, Launchpad, DirectionReadout); `keyboard/`, `a11y/`; `styles/tokens.css` (the whole visual vocabulary); `e2e/hormuz.spec.ts`.

**Tests: 259 on the server, 177 in the browser (one skipped on purpose — it waits for the join), one keyboard-only end-to-end test.** Continuous integration: `backend`, `frontend`, `types-fresh`, `docker`, `e2e` — **no API key in any of them**.

**What the engine says about Hormuz** (seed 20261001): *"Hormuz opens, then Iran is struck" moves [the Polymarket Brent contract] from .50 to .42 by 2026-10-04 and leaves 1 claim untouched.* A world costs about 65 ms, a difference about 200 ms.

**(History — stack 04 closed on 2026-09-21; see `RESUME-ux-round.md`.)** Then: stack **04**, as two parallel stacks — **04a** (browser: the join, then the map drawing itself) and **04b** (server: chapters + record 0015, the pipeline, the stream + replay, evals + ensemble + spread). Plan: `stack-04-generation.md`. **Kent answered every open question on 2026-09-17 — `plans/notes/2026-09-17-kent-decisions-stack-04.md` — and the plan is rewritten to match. Nothing is waiting on him.**

---

## 3. Read these, in this order (about 50 minutes)

1. `AGENTS.md` — the rules of the repo and the working agreements. **Binding.**
2. `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` — §1, §3 (eleven decisions — do not reopen them), §6.1–§6.2 (what generation must do), §7 (UX-1 to UX-14), §9 (fourteen invariants), §10 (anti-patterns), §12.
3. `ARCHITECTURE.md` — especially §2 (the model proposes; our code disposes) and §3 (the eight steps of a generation, with what is already built marked). **You must update it in the same pull request that makes a section real.**
4. `spec/README.md`, `spec/vocabulary.md`, then `spec/multiverse/interventions.md` (the feedback-arrow rule and the refusal codes), `propagation.md` B4–B7, `diff.md` (including **open question 7**), and `spec/workbench/README.md` + `diff-view.md` (the `WorldSource` seam).
5. `docs/adr/README.md`, then records **0006** (the model boundary — the verified API specifics), **0008**, **0012** (replay mode), **0003**, **0014**.
6. **`plans/notes/2026-09-17-kent-decisions-stack-03-round-2.md`** — eleven decisions and fourteen small ones. Binding on every later stack. Then **`plans/notes/2026-09-17-kent-decisions-stack-04.md`** — six decisions and eight small ones for stack 04.
7. `plans/history/stack-04-generation.md` (closed 2026-09-21) — then **`plans/RESUME-ux-round.md`**, which is where work resumes.

---

## 4. How Kent works — the rules that will get your work rejected if you break them

**Build aggressively through milestones.** Kent's own words: *"build aggressively through milestones, I edit after the fact."* He is a co-developer, not an approver standing at a gate. Decision records and spec chapters still come first in the *stack order* — the bottom pull request of every stack is docs-only — but code above them proceeds while he reads. Nothing here is irreversible.

**Push and open pull requests freely. Kent merges** — or asks the coordinator to, as he did for all of stack 03; then use §5. Never merge without being asked.

**All sub-agents run on Opus.** Kent said so directly. Do not downgrade a sub-agent to save tokens.

**Decisions come before code.** A significant architectural choice needs a decision record (`docs/adr/`, next number **0015**, copy `template.md`). Write it `proposed`, ask Kent, build only after he accepts. Small tooling choices already covered by a record need no new one.

**How to ask him — this worked.** Collect the open questions; have a read-only Opus agent analyse them for *the most principled, simplest-to-maintain design, balanced against functionality*, sorting them into "needs Kent" and "falls out of something already decided"; then put the first group to him with the **question tool**: each in plain words with the Hormuz example, what changes on screen and in code, the recommended option first. He settled eleven questions and approved fourteen small ones in one sitting. Record the answers in a dated note under `plans/notes/` and fold them into the chapters the same day.

**Two things Kent will veto on sight.**
1. **A template-looking interface.** Default component-library styling, a spinner followed by a dump of results, pop-up dialogs, a tangled hairball graph. His first reaction to the first canvas was "closer to spare than rich" — density and deliberate detail are wanted.
2. **Not knowing why it did that.** Any state that cannot be traced to an input, a rule, or a cited source. This applies to the product *and* to your own work: a number nobody computed is never typed by hand — not in a fixture, not in a chapter, not in a test.

**Write plainly.** No unexplained jargon, abbreviations, or symbols; each passage stands alone; short and punchy. When you cite an invariant such as INV-4, add a few words saying what it means.

**The spec is a book; decision records are a journal.** Do not number spec files. A journal entry's measurements are dated facts — add a dated note rather than rewriting them; a book chapter is kept true.

**Authority stays with Kent.** Offer options with a recommendation; do not argue him into things. If you take a call on his behalf, say so, say why, and make it easy to overturn. Questions go at the bottom of `STATUS.md` under "Waiting on Kent" **and in chat**, because he does not read `plans/` unprompted.

---

## 5. Git and pull requests (decision record 0009)

- **Branch names:** `<type>/<NN>-<slug>` — `feat/04a-join`, `spec/04b-generation`.
- **Commit messages:** Conventional Commits — `feat:`, `fix:`, `refactor:`, `test:`, `docs:`, `chore:`, `ci:`, plus `spec:` and `adr:`. End agent-written commits with the co-author line your session instructions give you.
- **Stacks:** bottom pull request targets `main`; each above targets its parent — `gh pr create --base <parent-branch>`. **At most four deep** — which is why stack 04 is two stacks.
- **Pull request body, three headings:** *What* · *Which invariant it satisfies* · *What is deliberately not here*. End with the generated-with line your session instructions give you.
- **Never commit or push to `main` directly.**

### Keep child branches linear — it decides how painful the merge is

When a parent branch gains commits after its child was cut, **rebase the child onto the parent** (the child is unpushed or yours alone) rather than merging the parent in. Stack 03 learned this the expensive way; see below.

### Merging a stack — what actually happens (learned 2026-09-17, twice)

**`gh pr merge` refuses a stacked pull request**, and on the top of a stack it silently merges into the parent branch instead of `main`. Never use it on a stack. Merge **bottom-up** through the async route; `plans/scripts/land.sh <pr> "<title>" <message-file>` does the waiting and polling:

```bash
gh api -X PUT repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async -f merge_method=squash \
  -f commit_title="<subject> (#<n>)" -f commit_message="<the What, as prose>" -f sha=<head sha>
gh api repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async/<uuid>      # poll until "merged"
```

After a parent merges:

1. **A linear child is restacked by GitHub itself** within about half a minute: rebased onto `main`, base retargeted to `main`. Your local copy of that branch is now behind a rewritten remote — check the trees are identical (`git diff --quiet origin/<b> <b>`) and `git reset --hard origin/<b>`. Then wait for checks and merge.
2. **A child carrying merge commits is not restacked.** Two cases:
   - *It is a strict superset of `main`* (it merged its parents in as they were first written). Prove it — the merged pull requests' original tips are ancestors, and `git diff --stat origin/main HEAD` lists only this pull request's files. A plain `git merge origin/main` will conflict on every file both sides touched (add/add against the squashed copies), so record the merge with `git merge -s ours origin/main`, confirm the tree did not change, push, `gh pr edit <n> --base main`.
   - *It is not a superset* (main moved for other reasons). `git rebase --onto origin/main <old-parent-tip> <branch>`, confirm `git diff --stat <reviewed-tip> HEAD -- <your dirs>` is empty, `git push --force-with-lease`, `gh pr edit <n> --base main`.
3. **Run a join check before merging the second of two parallel stacks**: both test suites and the end-to-end test on the rebased top branch. In stack 03 it caught an end-to-end assertion that typed in a fixture number the other stack had changed.
4. **After changing a pull request's base by hand, GitHub can keep a stale `CONFLICTING` and schedule no checks at all** (stack 04, #39): confirm `gh pr view <n> --json mergeable` is `MERGEABLE` and that `gh pr checks <n>` lists jobs BEFORE waiting on them; if not, `gh pr close <n> && gh pr reopen <n>` makes it recompute and run CI. GitHub also did not restack a child whose branch had been force-pushed — use the `rebase --onto` route above and prove the tree is identical to the reviewed tip.
5. Afterwards: delete branches locally and with `gh api -X DELETE repos/kgang/katalyst/git/refs/heads/<branch>`, `git worktree remove` each worktree, `git fetch --prune`. Leave the `entire/*` branches alone — they are the checkpoint tool's.

---

## 6. Your environment (checked 2026-09-17)

| Tool | Version here | Note |
|------|--------------|------|
| `gh` | 2.101.0, signed in as `kgang` | Repo `kgang/katalyst`, private |
| `uv` | 0.12.15 | |
| Python | 3.12.4 | |
| Node | 23.3.0 locally | Docker and CI pin **24**. Use `npm ci`, not `npm install`, in a fresh worktree |
| Docker | 27.5.1 | |
| Playwright | `@playwright/test` in `frontend/` | `npx playwright install chromium` once; `npx playwright test` starts both halves itself |

**`.env` in the main checkout is Kent's.** It is git-ignored and holds his real keys. **Never copy it into a worktree, never read it into a brief, never commit it.** `.env.example` is the one agents use.

**Hooks:** `.claude/settings.json` runs the `entire` checkpoint tool on session events; its output on `git push` is normal. The git hooks directory has a `commit-msg` hook but **no `pre-commit` hook wired**, so the linters do not run on commit — run `uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check .` and `npm run lint` yourself before committing.

**Model API key: stack 04b needs one to record cassettes and demos — and Kent must name a spending ceiling first.** Before writing *any* code that calls Claude, load the `claude-api` skill; decision record 0006 holds the verified specifics, and memory is unreliable. Continuous integration never gets a key.

**Running the app to look at it:** backend `cd backend && env -u ANTHROPIC_API_KEY -u FRED_API_KEY uv run uvicorn katalyst.api.main:app --port 80NN`; frontend `KATALYST_API_URL=http://localhost:80NN npm run dev -- --port 51NN --strictPort`. Give each agent its own pair of ports. For screenshots, a throwaway Playwright script **outside the repo** (the session scratchpad) at 1600 × 1000.

---

## 7. The worktree pattern

Every sub-agent gets its own checkout of its own branch under **`../katalyst-wt/<branch-slug>/`**. The main checkout stays on `main` and is never used by a sub-agent.

- **One agent per worktree**, except chapter writers, who may share one **only** when their files are disjoint and **none of them runs a git command** — the coordinator commits for them.
- **Disjoint owned files**, listed in the brief. "Touch nothing outside it. If something outside it must change, write why in your report."
- **Agents never push, never open a pull request, never touch `main`.** The coordinator reviews, then pushes and opens the pull request.
- A resumed agent (send it a message) keeps its context — use that for fix rounds and for sweeps of files it wrote. You can point a resumed agent at a *different* worktree when the fix has to land on another branch.
- Remove worktrees after the merge.

---

## 8. Lessons — read these twice

1. **After any interruption, check reality before acting.** `git log --oneline -5`, `git status`, `git worktree list`, `gh pr list`, and `STATUS.md`. Do not trust your memory of the repo; trust the repo.
2. **Append to `STATUS.md` before you stop**, and whenever the set of open pull requests or running agents changes. Record Kent's instructions there in his own words.
3. **Brief sub-agents fully, and point at the one copy.** They know only what you tell them. Give the plan and the decisions note by **absolute path in the main checkout** (readable from any worktree) rather than pasting tables — no transcription drift. Paste only what must be word for word on screen.
4. **Keep cross-references consistent.** After any rename or any changed number, search the whole repo. A fixture change in stack 03 made numbers stale in eight chapters, the PRD, a decision record and an end-to-end test.
5. **Whoever changes a fixture or an engine rule lists which chapter numbers went stale, and the sweep travels in the same pull request.** Resume the chapter's own writer for the sweep.
6. **Verify every sub-agent's claim yourself.** Run the tests and lints, read the diff against the owned-files list, hand-check arithmetic on a tiny map of your own, **launch the app and look**. A report is a hypothesis. In stack 03 this caught: a lint failure an agent reported as green, a plate overlap on a map the agent had not probed, and a fixed-height tile full of dead space.
7. **Write the shapes sheet before parallel writers start** — and for parallel stacks, the event or type vocabulary they share.
8. **Put a read-only reviewer over parallel writers, every time.** It found about ten blocking cross-chapter disagreements per stack — two names for one type, the same test named two ways, "six options" over a list of five, a block of invented numbers. Have it **re-do every worked number by hand from the fixture**.
9. **Two honest principles settle most small questions**: one rule over two (find the rule the code already obeys and name it once); and a code, a word or a number must mean what it says (that is why there is `edit_not_applicable`, why `killed` means only forced false, why the chip says "stated range · not computed").
10. **Never put a typed-in number where a computed one belongs — including in tests.** Assert directions, orderings and states; or compare a value with itself across a change.
11. **Property tests must build their inputs.** One that `assume()`s most inputs away fails Hypothesis's health check in CI on a bad seed while passing locally. CI is about 2.5× slower than this machine.
12. **The first pull request of a stack is small enough to write yourself**: commit chapter *stubs* (headings only) so code agents can branch off the spec branch at once.
13. **Opus agents can hit a session limit** ("resets 7am America/New_York"). If one dies, check disk state before reviving it by message.
15. **A client library accepting a shape proves nothing about the service.** In stack 04 the SDK built a schema from a union of three shapes without complaint and the service refused it on the first live call (`For 'anyOf', '$defs' is not supported`). Only a live call settles a vendor question — make the first one early, make it small, and do not close a chapter's open question on the library's say-so.
16. **Test a program as a program, and make a paid run impossible to lose.** Twice in stack 04 a run that cost money kept nothing: once because the recorder threw the receipt away with a file it would not write, once because the module's `__main__` guard sat above a function it called — invisible to every test (tests import, so everything is defined first) and to ruff and mypy. Run each `python -m` entry point in a subprocess test through its whole path; keep anything paid for incrementally, so a crash still leaves a file.
17. **A rare test failure is a bug until the evidence says otherwise.** Four times in stack 04 an agent's first instinct was "flaky — clear the example database": the keyboard left behind on a rebuilt tile; two keys in one frame; a locality leak through the day grid (a claim in a separate piece of the map moved by `.096`); a second through one global survival mask (`.083`). Every one was a real defect a user could hit. Find the falsifying input, rebuild it by hand, and decide with evidence whether the test or the product is wrong. And pytest TRUNCATES a repr — `Belief(p=1.85...` is `1.85e-05`, not a likelihood above 1.
18. **Several worktrees on one machine share one set of end-to-end ports.** Until stack 04 fixed it, `frontend/playwright.config.ts` used fixed ports and reused any server already up, so one agent's `npx playwright test` silently tested another branch's app — and "verified" numbers were wrong in both directions. Give every agent, and yourself, explicit ports (`KATALYST_E2E_BACKEND_PORT`, `KATALYST_E2E_FRONTEND_PORT`), never reuse a server, and never edit a source file under a running dev server (a hot reload blanks the page mid-test and looks like your change broke everything).
19. **One queue for heavy work, enforced by a script, not by asking.** Stack 04's first session ran three or four suites and 40× repeat bars at once; the load sat at 20–23 and the load itself caused failures that were then chased. `plans/scripts/heavy.sh` is a lock directory holding its owner's process id: whoever asks waits their turn. Agents run single test files, linters and type checks directly; a whole suite through the queue; playwright, repeat bars and anything paid are the coordinator's alone. Two 600-run bars and four agents' suites went through it on 2026-09-21 without one spurious failure.
20. **100% coverage and 259 green tests proved nothing about whether the arithmetic was right.** Three defects sat on the demo map — an observation that never reached a cause, endings deaf to half their causes, a supposition voided by a claim nobody believed — because no test compared the engine with an answer worked out independently, under an edit. Every engine needs an oracle that is *forbidden the engine's internals*, the way the locality oracle may not call `affected_set`. And check what an oracle can see: one that shares the core's tables proves the summing and is blind to a wrong table.
21. **Attack a plan before its owner sees it, and re-check a review before acting on it.** The two midpoint reviews read a `main` ten pull requests old: of one audit's blockers, six were already fixed, and one review's central claim about generation (the map is a tree) was false by measurement. Then the coordinator's own synthesis said "solved exactly" where an adversarial pass measured .12 of error, offered Kent a choice that was not optional, and under-counted the work by about 1.6×. One read-only red-team agent, told to break it, cost twenty minutes. A design that rests on a prototype opens with a spike and a kill criterion. And keep the evidence: an analyst's scripts go in `plans/analysis/scripts/`, not a temp directory.
22. **A green bar here is not a green bar there — and more runs of the same bar is not the answer.** On 2026-09-21 a replay test passed 20 cold runs of 20 on this machine and failed the build's FIRST run: the layout is worked out on its own thread, the build machine's thread was slower, and a claim took a rectangle's place at the origin. Throttling the processor did not reproduce it (that slows the page, not the layout thread); starting the layout thread 900 ms late did, at once. The same day a generated numbers file matched byte for byte across macOS/Arm and Linux/x86-64 — and its own margin test still went red on Linux, because with 280 numbers some value sits on a rounding boundary on some machine at ANY digit count. **Rules:** a test that reads a MOMENT (what stood when X arrived) gets a no-browser twin that injects the bad timing on purpose; a check that compares NUMBERS uses a stated tolerance, never text; and the amount of browser testing follows the three tiers in `PLAN.md`'s working rules — one cold run and the build by default, a repeat bar only for a rare failure that has actually been seen. The "20 cold runs" bar was never a recorded standard; it cost about fifty-two minutes that day (twice in full, a third time to five runs of twenty) and caught nothing one run plus the build would not have.
23. **The whole suite, through the queue, before EVERY push; and never edit a worktree while a bar is running in it.** Both broken once on 2026-09-21: a push after two test files let three stale health tests reach the build (#41's first run); an edit under a running bar hot-reloaded a fix into its dev server and voided three runs. Check `plans/.heavy.log` for an open START before touching a worktree.
24. **A defect an agent "fixed" without a browser is a hypothesis — revert the fix and watch the test go red before believing either.** Stack 04's polish branch boasted that its new layout check *"found its first defect before it was ever run"*: three fields overflowing the panel. With both "fixes" reverted the fields still sat inside it — `width: 100%` had always been there — and the check written to catch the overflow could not have seen one (the panel scrolls sideways, so scrolling a field into view made it measure as inside). Four deliberate breakages through the queue settled both in ten minutes.
25. **Anything paid is kept OUTSIDE the worktree that ran it.** `KATALYST_RUNS=/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/backend/.runs`. The raw run behind the committed Hormuz recording died with a removed worktree, and `docs/measurements.md` has to say so. And a program that writes its kept run only when a case ENDS loses it to a hard kill.
26. **Before writing "X says why", open X.** In one evening the coordinator wrote that a scorecard row named its effort (it did not — only the kept run did) and glossed a stop reason from its name (`width_cap` is not "the map reached its widest"). Both were caught only by looking. A sentence about what a file holds is a claim like any other.
27. **The suite had never met a live run, a keyed first screen, or a generated map — and Kent met all three in his first five minutes.** Every browser test plays a recording at 0.4 s an event, with an empty key, over the one curated map where every number exists. So a dead `?` key, a minute of silence after pressing *Watch it build*, a recording unreachable with a key, and 36 empty cells of 54 on the tiles were all invisible to 1 000 green tests. **Walk the product the way its owner will — with the key in, on a map nobody curated — before calling a stack done.** And when analysts plan the fix, put what the owner literally asked for on the table at full strength beside their alternative: three of four had quietly argued him out of it, and an adversarial pass re-counted their ~12 sessions at ~25.
14. **Say what you merged and why before Kent has to ask**, and if you take a step earlier than he literally asked (stack 03a was merged while 03b's last pull request was still being built), tell him plainly and offer to hold.

---

## 9. The road from here

| Stack | What it proves | Plan |
|-------|----------------|------|
| ~~01 skeleton~~ · ~~02 schema~~ | **Merged.** | history |
| ~~03a engine ∥ 03b canvas~~ | **Merged 2026-09-17.** Changing one step re-computes only what is downstream; the map is dense, readable and keyboard-driven | `stack-03a-engine.md`, `stack-03b-canvas.md` (history) |
| ~~04a join + growth ∥ 04b generation~~ | **Merged; closed 2026-09-21** (`history/stack-04-generation.md`). The canvas shows the engine's numbers; the model draws a real map for any hypothesis, streamed step by step; with no key the four examples replay | `stack-04-generation.md` |
| 05 thesis | The map compiles to a trade with a derived stop-loss and live market prices | `roadmap-03-to-06.md` |
| 06 probes | Extra modeling effort where the user points it (stretch) | `roadmap-03-to-06.md` |
| 07 presentable (proposed) | README walkthrough, a pastcast self-test, a last accessibility sweep | `roadmap-03-to-06.md` |

**This table is history as of 2026-09-21. Start with `PLAN.md`** — stacks 05, 06 and 07 mean different things now, and several of their lines wait on Kent (`notes/2026-09-21-decisions-after-review.md`).

#!/bin/bash
# heavy.sh <label> -- <command...>
#
# The one queue for anything heavy on this machine: a whole test suite, a browser
# run, a repeat bar. It waits its turn, runs the command, and gives the turn back.
# One at a time, whoever asks. Last session three or four suites ran together, the
# load sat at 20-23, and the load itself caused "flaky" failures that then had to
# be chased (STATUS 2026-09-21).
#
# The turn is a directory (making one is atomic). It holds the owner's process id,
# so a turn left behind by a killed run is taken back rather than waited on for ever.
#
# NOT for a single test file, a linter or a type check: run those directly.
set -uo pipefail
LOCK=/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/.heavy.lock
LOG=/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/.heavy.log
LABEL=${1:?usage: heavy.sh <label> -- <command...>}; shift
[ "${1:-}" = "--" ] && shift
waited=0
until mkdir "$LOCK" 2>/dev/null; do
  owner=$(cat "$LOCK/pid" 2>/dev/null || echo "")
  if [ -n "$owner" ] && ! kill -0 "$owner" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "heavy: taking back a turn left by dead process $owner ($(cat "$LOCK/label" 2>/dev/null))" >&2
    rm -rf "$LOCK"; continue
  fi
  [ $((waited % 60)) -eq 0 ] && echo "heavy: '$LABEL' waiting behind '$(cat "$LOCK/label" 2>/dev/null)' (${waited}s)" >&2
  sleep 5; waited=$((waited + 5))
done
echo $$ > "$LOCK/pid"; echo "$LABEL" > "$LOCK/label"
trap 'rm -rf "$LOCK"' EXIT
start=$(date +%s)
echo "$(date '+%H:%M:%S') START $LABEL (waited ${waited}s, load $(sysctl -n vm.loadavg | awk '{print $2}'))" >> "$LOG"
"$@"; code=$?
echo "$(date '+%H:%M:%S') END   $LABEL exit=$code took=$(( $(date +%s) - start ))s" >> "$LOG"
exit $code

#!/bin/bash
# land.sh <pr> <title> <message-file>
# GitHub restacks a child branch onto main by itself when its parent merges, so this only:
# checks the base is main and the branch sits on main, waits for the four checks, squash-merges via the async route.
set -euo pipefail
PR=$1; TITLE=$2; MSG=$3
cd /Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst
for i in $(seq 1 12); do BASE=$(gh pr view $PR --json baseRefName -q .baseRefName); [ "$BASE" = "main" ] && break; sleep 5; done
[ "$BASE" = "main" ] || { echo "base is $BASE, not main"; exit 3; }
git fetch -q origin
HEAD_SHA=$(gh pr view $PR --json headRefOid -q .headRefOid)
git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/main $HEAD_SHA || { echo "head $HEAD_SHA does not sit on main yet"; exit 5; }
echo "head ${HEAD_SHA:0:7} sits on main; waiting for checks…"
for i in $(seq 1 90); do
  out=$(gh pr checks $PR 2>&1 || true)
  if echo "$out" | grep -qw "fail"; then echo "CHECK FAILED:"; echo "$out"; exit 4; fi
  if ! echo "$out" | grep -qw "pending" && [ "$(echo "$out" | grep -cw pass)" -ge 4 ]; then break; fi
  sleep 10
done
gh pr checks $PR | awk '{print $1"="$2}' | tr '\n' ' '; echo
[ "$(gh pr view $PR --json headRefOid -q .headRefOid)" = "$HEAD_SHA" ] || { echo "head moved while waiting"; exit 6; }
R=$(gh api -X PUT repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/$PR/merge-async -f merge_method=squash -f commit_title="$TITLE (#$PR)" -f commit_message="$(cat "$MSG")" -f sha=$HEAD_SHA)
UUID=$(echo "$R" | jq -r .details.uuid)
for i in $(seq 1 30); do r=$(gh api repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/$PR/merge-async/$UUID); [ "$(echo "$r" | jq -r .status)" != "pending" ] && break; sleep 5; done
echo "$r" | jq -c .

#!/bin/bash
# heavy.sh <label> -- <command...>
#
# The one queue for anything heavy on this machine: a whole test suite, a browser
# run, a repeat bar. It waits its turn, runs the command, and gives the turn back.
# One at a time, whoever asks. Last session three or four suites ran together, the
# load sat at 20-23, and the load itself caused "flaky" failures that then had to
# be chased (STATUS 2026-09-21).
#
# The turn is a directory (making one is atomic). It holds the owner's process id,
# so a turn left behind by a killed run is taken back rather than waited on for ever.
#
# NOT for a single test file, a linter or a type check: run those directly.
set -uo pipefail
LOCK=/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/.heavy.lock
LOG=/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/.heavy.log
LABEL=${1:?usage: heavy.sh <label> -- <command...>}; shift
[ "${1:-}" = "--" ] && shift
waited=0
until mkdir "$LOCK" 2>/dev/null; do
  owner=$(cat "$LOCK/pid" 2>/dev/null || echo "")
  if [ -n "$owner" ] && ! kill -0 "$owner" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "heavy: taking back a turn left by dead process $owner ($(cat "$LOCK/label" 2>/dev/null))" >&2
    rm -rf "$LOCK"; continue
  fi
  [ $((waited % 60)) -eq 0 ] && echo "heavy: '$LABEL' waiting behind '$(cat "$LOCK/label" 2>/dev/null)' (${waited}s)" >&2
  sleep 5; waited=$((waited + 5))
done
echo $$ > "$LOCK/pid"; echo "$LABEL" > "$LOCK/label"
trap 'rm -rf "$LOCK"' EXIT
start=$(date +%s)
echo "$(date '+%H:%M:%S') START $LABEL (waited ${waited}s, load $(sysctl -n vm.loadavg | awk '{print $2}'))" >> "$LOG"
"$@"; code=$?
echo "$(date '+%H:%M:%S') END   $LABEL exit=$code took=$(( $(date +%s) - start ))s" >> "$LOG"
exit $code

#!/bin/bash
# land.sh <pr> <title> <message-file>
# GitHub restacks a child branch onto main by itself when its parent merges, so this only:
# checks the base is main and the branch sits on main, waits for the four checks, squash-merges via the async route.
set -euo pipefail
PR=$1; TITLE=$2; MSG=$3
cd /Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst
for i in $(seq 1 12); do BASE=$(gh pr view $PR --json baseRefName -q .baseRefName); [ "$BASE" = "main" ] && break; sleep 5; done
[ "$BASE" = "main" ] || { echo "base is $BASE, not main"; exit 3; }
git fetch -q origin
HEAD_SHA=$(gh pr view $PR --json headRefOid -q .headRefOid)
git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/main $HEAD_SHA || { echo "head $HEAD_SHA does not sit on main yet"; exit 5; }
echo "head ${HEAD_SHA:0:7} sits on main; waiting for checks…"
for i in $(seq 1 90); do
  out=$(gh pr checks $PR 2>&1 || true)
  if echo "$out" | grep -qw "fail"; then echo "CHECK FAILED:"; echo "$out"; exit 4; fi
  if ! echo "$out" | grep -qw "pending" && [ "$(echo "$out" | grep -cw pass)" -ge 4 ]; then break; fi
  sleep 10
done
gh pr checks $PR | awk '{print $1"="$2}' | tr '\n' ' '; echo
[ "$(gh pr view $PR --json headRefOid -q .headRefOid)" = "$HEAD_SHA" ] || { echo "head moved while waiting"; exit 6; }
R=$(gh api -X PUT repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/$PR/merge-async -f merge_method=squash -f commit_title="$TITLE (#$PR)" -f commit_message="$(cat "$MSG")" -f sha=$HEAD_SHA)
UUID=$(echo "$R" | jq -r .details.uuid)
for i in $(seq 1 30); do r=$(gh api repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/$PR/merge-async/$UUID); [ "$(echo "$r" | jq -r .status)" != "pending" ] && break; sleep 5; done
echo "$r" | jq -c .

# The brief every stack-04 agent gets (read this first, fully)

**Who you are and what this is.** You are one Opus sub-agent on Katalyst, a take-home prototype for Catalyst (catalyst.app): you type an event you think will happen; Katalyst shows what it would cause, step by step, ending in trades, and lets you change any step to see how the trades change. The owner is Kent Gang, a solo developer. He cares about structure with Docker and tests, proper code design, rigorously documented decisions, and a beautiful interface. **He vetoes two things on sight:** a template-looking interface (default component styling, a spinner then a dump, pop-up dialogs, a hair

**Read first, in this order.**
1. `AGENTS.md` in your worktree. Binding.
2. The plan, by absolute path: `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/stack-04-generation.md`. Read its first paragraph, "How 04a and 04b stay out of each other's way", "The shapes sheet", "Pre-decisions", and **your own pull request's section**. `plans/` is git-ignored, so you can only reach it by that absolute path.
3. Kent's decisions, both binding, reopen nothing: `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/notes/2026-09-17-kent-decisions-stack-04.md` (G1–G6, S1–S8) and `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/notes/2026-09-17-kent-decisions-stack-03-round-2.md` (K1–K11 and fourteen small ones).
4. `spec/README.md` (the chapter shape) and `spec/vocabulary.md` including the Interface words table and "Words for a number that is not there".
5. Whatever your own section below adds.

**House rules.**
- Plain words everywhere, including docstrings and comments: no unexplained jargon, abbreviations or symbols; each passage stands alone; short and punchy. When you cite an invariant such as INV-4, add a few words saying what it means. Use `spec/vocabulary.md`'s words exactly. No code name — `do`, `observe`, `insert`, `retune`, `refine`, `believe` — ever appears on screen.
- Reject, never repair. One rule over two: find the rule the code already obeys and name it once. A code, a word or a number must mean what it says.
- **Never put a typed-in number where a computed one belongs — including in tests.** Assert directions, orderings and states; or compare a value with itself across a change. Any number you quote in a chapter you must have measured from the engine yourself, and say how.
- Property tests must **build** their inputs, never `assume()` most of them away. Continuous integration is about 2.5× slower than this machine.
- Every module, class and function has a plain-words docstring saying what it is for and what it must never do.
- The spec is a book (kept true, files not numbered); decision records are a journal (dated amendments, never rewrite a measurement).
- **Never read, copy or print `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/.env`.** You have no model key and need none. **You never run anything that calls a model or spends money.** Use `.env.example`. Run servers with `env -u ANTHROPIC_API_KEY -u FRED_API_KEY`.
- Before writing any code that calls Claude, load the `claude-api` skill and verify every model name, parameter and price against it and against decision record 0006. Never from memory.

**Git.** Work only in your worktree on your branch. Conventional Commits (`feat:`, `fix:`, `test:`, `docs:`, `spec:`, `adr:` …) ending with the line `Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>`. **Do not push. Do not open a pull request. Do not touch `main`. Do not touch any other worktree.** If your section says "no git", run no git command that changes anything — the coordinator commits for you. No pre-commit hook runs the linters: run them yourself.

**Files you own** are listed in your section. Touch nothing outside them. If something outside must change, write why in your report and stop short of changing it.

**Verify before reporting.** Server: from `backend/`, `uv run pytest`, `uv run ruff check .`, `uv run ruff format --check .`, `uv run mypy --strict src/katalyst/domain`. Browser: from `frontend/`, `npm ci` once, then `npm run check`; launch the app and **screenshot every state you built** at 1600 × 1000 with a throwaway Playwright script kept outside the repo, in the scratch directory your section names; then run the visual review checklist in `spec/workbench/README.md` on your own pictures. "It looks good" without pictures is not finished.

**Report format** (your final message): *What I built* · *Where I deviated from the plan and why* · *Which chapter numbers my change made stale* · *Open questions* · *Files touched* (from `git diff --stat` against your base) · the exact output tail of each verification command.

**Four traps.** (a) The model must be structurally unable to mint an identifier or declare provenance — if you find yourself validating that it did not, the schema is wrong. (b) A rejected proposal is an event, not an error. (c) A belief chip resolves once, at the end. (d) *Agreement* means the diff's same-direction share and nothing else; there is no run-to-run number in this stack.

7	## 1. What is true today
8	
9	**The foot of a generating map has three strips and none is about the run:** *last key* (`MapFrame.tsx:116`), the live region (`:138`), the provenance line (`:147`).
10	
11	**The one sentence about the run is invisible.** `GenerationScreen.tsx:304` passes `spokenOnly={true}` and `components/generationDock.css:38-48` clips `.map-live--spoken` to one pixel, so *"Asked for a map of … A rectangle is held open where the first claim will go"* (`a11y/growth.ts:42-47`) is spoken and never shown. `e2e/generate.spec.ts:230` **asserts** that hiding, which is why no test could have caught it.
12	
13	**The provenance line asserts arrivals on an empty map.** `stream/growth.ts:192-200` writes *"Every claim and arrow on this map arrived from /api/generate…"* from `generation_started` onward — before one claim exists (`plans/logs/m4-look/02-one-second-after.png`).
14	
15	**"Read the working of this run →" is offered from the first event and never resolves.** The control renders whenever `generationId !== null` (`GenerationScreen.tsx:346`), but the fetch is gated on `finished` (`GenerationScreen.tsx:96-99`), so pressing it mid-run leaves *"Reading the working of this run back from the server…"* (`components/Inspector.tsx:905-909`) until the run ends.
16	
17	**How long the silences are.** Measured: `medium` effort, **51.98 s per call** (`plans/logs/eval-hormuz-medium.log`); the recorder's effort, **109.65 s per call** (`plans/logs/eval-hormuz.log`). A round asks three claims at once (`engine/outcome.py:311`, `at_once: 3`), so events land in bursts of up to three and the screen is then still for about a minute.
18	
19	**What the server knows and does not say.** Nothing records that a call went out: `grow.py:243-256` submits a round to a thread pool and the next thing anyone sees is an answer; `following.py:109-115` folds only returned answers. So *which claim is open* is on the wire (`frontier`, on both growth events — `engine/events.py:114,143`) and *which three are in flight*, *whether a search is running*, *call number* and *tokens so far* are not on it at all. Calls, tokens and searches arrive on the receipt, second-to-last (`engine/events.py:166-217`). Polling the transcript adds nothing: `transcript.py:60-120` gains a line only when a call *returns*, and every returning call that changes the map already made an event.

Measured: **0 pin drops in 25, 14 and 12 passes.** A tile reserves its belief rail while the map grows (`geometry.ts:177`), so `beliefs_propagated` changes no height and drops no pin. **INV-workbench.64's note that "every tile gains a chip and so every tile can change height" does not describe what happens** — the whole run is one unbroken chain of pins.

| Lane | Branch | What it is doing |
|---|---|---|
| **K** | `fix/04-the-question-mark` | Moves `?`, `⌘K` and `Escape` into `keyboard/everyKey.ts` so they work on all three screens, and adds a `?` press to the replay walk |
| **D1** | `adr/04-what-the-run-says-and-when-a-tile-moves` | Writes records 0023 and 0024 as `proposed` and edits `streaming-growth.md` once for both |
| **D2** | `adr/04-what-a-start-is` | Amends record 0012, adds `first-screen.md`, then adds the `replay`/`live` field in separate commits |
| **4** | `feat/04-the-quieter-tile` | Hides empty user and market columns, rewrites the apple and dominoes sentences tersely, adds `VR14` |

  - run strip on K, then the settle on the strip;
  - the server field on D2's docs, then the first screen on that.

He pressed *Watch it build* with a key and saw nothing for ~23 s, then events ~50–110 s apart, with one dim *HELD OPEN* rectangle between. ## Build

1. **One strip at the foot of both map screens** carrying the sentence the screen reader already hears, made visible. Delete `spokenOnly` and the one-pixel clip (`components/generationDock.css` ~38–48) — remove, do not guard.

3.
